In addition to the constructive macro tone in the January 31, 2018 FOMC statement (solid activity, strong labor market, inflation still below but moving toward 2 percent), the latest SLOOS around this period points to broadly supportive—but not uniformly easy—credit conditions. Banks reported standards for C&I loans to large and middle‑market firms as unchanged to slightly easier with terms competitive, while CRE standards remained somewhat tighter and demand softer. On the household side, standards for some consumer credit (notably credit cards and autos) had tightened on net, with mixed demand; mortgage standards were little changed to modestly easier in select categories. This pattern implies the credit channel is still transmitting support to business investment but offers less tailwind to household spending and CRE, consistent with a cautiously constructive outlook.

Taken together, the FOMC’s gradualism and forward guidance remain appropriate in a New Keynesian/Taylor-rule framing, and the Desk’s administered-rate implementation remains aligned with a floor-system approach. However, SLOOS’ pockets of tightening—especially in consumer and CRE—tilt risks modestly more cautious than a purely macro read would suggest, complementing Financial Stability Report observations of elevated valuations and higher nonfinancial business leverage. Net effect: outlook still positive and rule-like, but with a slightly more guarded bias.
